The land is small, just 0.21 hectares, but it is my own and I know every corner of it. For rice, I will buy what fertilizer I can find at the agro-dealer or through the government people, though it is never enough — maybe one or two bags for this plot — because without it the yield on this sandy soil is poor. I will also put cow dung from my animals, as we always do, to help the soil hold water. I keep my own seed from last year; the improved seeds are too costly and hard to find, and my own seed has always grown. I do not have chemicals for spraying — those are for cowpea and vegetable people, and we cannot afford them anyway. The rains will come soon, and I will depend on Allah and the rain; I have no pump or canal for watering. My wives and children will do most of the work — transplanting, weeding, scaring birds, and harvesting — but during the busy times I may call two or three young men from the village for a few days.
